articles.title_orig: 4 Cool New Features Your Fitbit Air Is Getting In October 2026
articles.title_zh: 4 Cool New Features Your Fitbit Air Is Getting In October 2026
articles.content_orig:
While the new Fitbit Edge is set to release in late October, the older Fitbit Air remains one of the best affordable fitness trackers you can buy today . It doesn't offer the same experience as a full smartwatch, but the Fitbit Air's comfortable build and versatile set of health and wellness tracking features make it a great alternative to Whoop and other screenless fitness bands.
While the Fitbit Air already comes with most features you'd want from a fitness tracker, Google recently announced several additions and improvements coming alongside the Fitbit Edge later in the month. These include the ability to passively track blood pressure trends, insulin resistance levels, and sleep breathing quality, which are all part of Google's new AI-based Health Guardian suite. Existing features like automatic workout detection are also being improved, and Google has also announced several partnerships with other health organizations to offer cross-platform compatibility with a variety of third-party services, devices, and apps. Some of these features are already rolling out, while users can expect others closer to the end of the month.
The American Heart Association labels hypertension (high blood pressure) as a 'silent killer' due to its lack of apparent symptoms until detected through screening. With nearly half of the adult population in the U.S. suffering from hypertension and being at risk of a heart attack or other health complications, monitoring blood pressure is extremely important — and Google is making it convenient for those with a Fitbit Air.
Google's new Health Guardian suite of features includes blood pressure trend tracking for users with a Google Health Premium subscription, which costs $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually. This uses the watch's optical heart rate and motion sensors alongside Google's WavesFM AI model to passively measure your blood pressure trends throughout the day and warn you of any risks on the first of every month. Google states that this isn't meant to replace a dedicated blood pressure measuring device, but it provides a proactive way to notice changes without having to visit a doctor. It's also worth noting that neither the Fitbit Air nor Google Pixel watches support on-demand blood pressure readings.
Blood pressure monitoring is nothing new in the wearable space. The 2021 Huawei Watch D offered background blood pressure tracking and on-demand measurements using a mechanical pump built into the watch, and U.S. owners of select Samsung Galaxy watches, such as the Galaxy Watch 9 (with an external pump), and owners of Apple wearables like the Apple Watch Series 12 also got the feature earlier this year. Google Pixel watches and the Fitbit Air were a notable exception until now.
Another frequently undetected condition that can pose severe risks is insulin resistance or impaired insulin sensitivity. Insulin regulates blood sugar by aiding cells in the absorption of glucose to produce energy, and consistent resistance to it can lead to conditions like prediabetes and Type 2 diabetes, as well as other health complications.
Google is adding insulin resistance monitoring to the Fitbit Air with Health Guardian for users with Google Health Premium. This uses data gathered throughout the month from many of the sensors already in the Fitbit — optical heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and an accelerometer — and warns you of any detected trends that may present potential risks. Until now, only the Google Pixel Watch 5 had this feature, and now the Fitbit Air is also set to receive it. However, note that this feature only provides trend data and cannot provide on-demand insulin or blood glucose levels.
Beyond the newly added health metrics coming with Health Guardian, Google has also greatly improved certain existing features. If you've ever forgotten to start tracking a workout on your Pixel Watch or Fitbit Air, you might've noticed that it often intelligently does so without any manual input. The feature responsible for this is automatic activity detection, which is getting a huge upgrade in October.
Google states that automatic activity detection is going to be twice as accurate. This is possible using an AI model that will analyze context, such as your daily habits, when and how you work out, and manually added data. The number of supported workouts has also been expanded: the feature could initially detect only 10 activities, a number that has now been increased to over 100. The updated list of workouts includes swimming, strength training, certain racket and team sports, and more.
The Fitbit Air is a capable fitness band, but a standalone wrist-based tracker can only do so much by itself. You'll ultimately have to rely on other apps and equipment for specialized measurements, and managing different sources of data can be annoying. Fortunately, Google partners with several third-party health platforms and gives users the ability to sync and import data from a variety of apps and devices.
For instance, users with an Abbott Lingo continuous glucose monitor will soon be able to sync data with Google Health on select Google wearables, including the Fitbit Air. MyFitnessPal Premium users will now also be able to share food-specific logs with Google Health, and your Fitbit Air will get the ability to import lab results directly from Function Health later in the year. Starting early next year, users will also be able to sync Flo Health data with their Fitbit Air to receive more personalized advice from the Google Health Coach.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: CNN’s Christiane Amanpour to depart network after 43 years
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal it later withdrew.
The court action removes one barrier to Mohammed standing trial before a military commission in 2028, where the death penalty is a possible punishment. He has been held at the U.S. base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.
Mohammed is accused of being the ringleader of the plot to crash hijacked planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
The other two men who appealed to the Supreme Court were Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, who are also held at Guantanamo and set to face trial.
The three men had agreed to a plea deal with military prosecutors in 2024, signed off on by a military commission judge, that would have given them life sentences.
But days later, then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rejected the proposal, saying he had the authority to override the deal.
Military courts said he had no such authority but, in an August ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled in favor of the government , prompting the men to appeal to the Supreme Court.
They argued, among other things, that the appeals court had no authority to intervene in the case.
The long delay in Mohammed facing trial was caused partly by concerns about evidence obtained via CIA torture.
A fourth alleged plotter earmarked for trial, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, was not involved in the appeal.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: 5 Ugreen Travel Gadgets Worth Adding To Your Long-Haul Flight Kit
articles.title_zh: 5 Ugreen Travel Gadgets Worth Adding To Your Long-Haul Flight Kit
articles.content_orig:
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Long-haul flights can be as tiresome and boring as they are exciting. Spending hours on a flight and at airports requires preparation to ensure you not only have fun during travel but also arrive at your destination with your phones and other devices topped up. This includes creating the perfect flight kit with tech gadgets like a long-lasting, TSA-approved power bank , a good set of noise-canceling headphones , an international travel adapter, and even tracking tags for peace of mind about the security of your prized possessions during your trip.
Luckily, you can find all these essential travel gadgets in one place: Ugreen. The popular consumer electronics brand sells a wide variety of charging accessories, as well as audio equipment and location trackers. That said, because it has a large library of products, it can be slightly confusing to know which ones to pick before you catch your next flight.
But we're here to help you. We've used our experience testing and comparing tech accessories to identify the top five Ugreen gadgets worth adding to your long-haul flight kit. These include a 20,000 mAh fast-charging wired power bank , a 10,000 mAh wireless power bank, a pair of over-ear headphones, and Ugreen's AirTag-like tracker tags. Even better, they're all budget-friendly and easily available on Amazon.
The Ugreen Nexode 20,000 mAh power bank is an ideal option for long-haul flights, even those that include long layovers. Its massive battery capacity means you can charge your devices multiple times before the power bank itself needs a recharge. According to Ugreen itself, the power bank can top up the iPhone 16 Pro 3.7 times, the Galaxy S25 Ultra three times, and even heavier-duty tech gadgets like the iPad Pro and MacBook Air more than once. At the time of writing, this budget-friendly power bank is available on Amazon for just $59.99, with a very strong 4.4-star rating after more than 5,500 reviews.
Another big selling point of this Ugreen power bank is its charging speed. It can deliver power at 100 W through its main USB-C outlet, which can juice up nearly any phone from 0% to 50% in less than half an hour. It also comes with a USB-C cable capable of supporting 100 W fast charging, so you don't have to spend extra. It's also got two other outlets: another USB-C with a 30 W output and one USB-A port with 22.5 W max output. In total, you can simultaneously charge three devices. Just note that in that case, the main USB-C port caps out at 65 W, which is still plenty fast.
Users also like how lightweight and compact this power bank is. It measures 5.47 by 3.23 by 1.02 inches and weighs just 0.925 pounds. One reviewer said, "it fits comfortably in a backpack and will charge multiple devices quickly." Lastly, we also like that the power bank itself charges quickly. It can charge at 65 W, going from nil to full in around two hours, according to Ugreen.
Although Ugreen is popular for its battery packs, docks, chargers, and other related accessories, it's also got a healthy lineup of headphones and earbuds. And the Ugreen HiTune Max5c wireless over ear headphones are a particularly great gadget for frequent flyers , thanks mainly to their value for money. They're priced at just $35.99 on Amazon, where they enjoy a solid 4.4-star rating after more than 2,200 reviews. According to expert hands-on testing at Hi-Tech.UA , their "sound is exactly at the level of models twice as expensive," while one everyday reviewer said that they're "similar quality to headphones that cost over $200."
They rock a 40 mm dynamic driver and offer punchy bass and surprisingly crisp highs. They're also certified to support Hi-Res audio, thanks to LDAC decoding, which reduces audio loss and latency during wireless transmission. Moreover, these are also noise-canceling headphones. They feature adaptive ANC with multiple modes, including complete isolation — Ugreen says its AI noise-canceling chip can reduce 43 dB of noise — and a transparency mode, giving you greater control over your surroundings. They can both dampen and totally eliminate the chatter around you during flights.
They also provide a comfortable fit. They've got a thick headband, big ear cushions that are made of soft leather and are easy to rotate (90-degree internal rotation and 15-degree external rotation) and extend, and a metal frame that makes them flexible yet robust. Despite their voluminous appearance, though, they weigh just 0.58 pounds, making them easy to wear for long periods. One reviewer said, "I watched two movies on the plane back to back with no pain." Lastly, the battery life is also great, at 75 hours with ANC off and 45 hours with ANC on.
Ugreen's FineTrack Mini 2 are small tracking devices that let you monitor the live location of your precious belongings, whether it's the hand luggage you take with you in the airplane cabin or your suitcases that often become difficult to find in that crowded conveyor belt, as well as other things like your wallet and keys. A pack of four (iOS only) currently costs just $31.99 on Amazon, with a 4.4-star rating after over 500 reviews. Even better, your purchase includes a keychain attachment case for each of the four air trackers.
One of their biggest pros is that they're compatible with Apple's Find My app , so you don't have to install any third-party application. Moreover, setup is seamless and straightforward. All you have to do is open Find My and add it as an object. And if you're running iOS 17 or later, you also have the ability to share the tracker's location with others. In addition to a long battery life of 5-7 years, they're also built to be easily found in the dark, courtesy of their fluorescent design.
They have an IP68 rating, so they can withstand harsh outdoor conditions, including heavy rain. We also like their alert system, which sends notification to you in the event your item has moved a bit too far. There's also an alarm feature, which produces loud 110 dB sounds at the press of a button to help you locate the tracker when it's nearby. One reviewer remarked that they're even louder than Apple's AirTags and called them "hands down a better buy than AirTags." For context, a pack of four AirTags costs around $99 — about thrice the price of Ugreen's air trackers.
A wireless power bank is the perfect fit for when you want to charge your phone on the flight without having to clutter your tray space with wires. The Ugreen MagFlow 10,000 mAh Qi2 wireless power bank , then, is worth your attention. It's compatible with the latest Qi2.2 wireless charging standard and can therefore charge any iPhone from iPhone 16 onward at 25 W, which is the fastest possible wireless charging speed available in Western markets right now. That equals 0-50% on the iPhone 17 Pro Max in around 38 minutes. It can also charge an iPhone 12-15, albeit at 15 W.
Right now, it's available on Amazon for $64.99, with a 4.5-star rating after more than 2,200 reviews. It comes with 17 magnets for easy snaps and solid grip. One reviewer said, "The magnetic hold is excellent. It stays securely attached to the phone and does not slide around." It can also function as a typical wired power bank, as it has two USB-C outlets capable of delivering 30 W of power output. One of them is the integrated USB-C cable that also functions as a carrying strap.
The power bank recharges at 30 W, meaning it'll take around two hours for a full recharge. Users also like the little display it comes with. "[It] helps keep track of how much juice we have left to squeeze," as one Amazon reviewer put it. It also has light indicators to show when wireless and fast charging are on or off. Additionally, it's convenient to carry around with you on flights. That's because it weighs just 0.56 pounds and measures 4.36 by 2.72 by 0.83 inches.

articles.title_orig: Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 fighters
articles.title_zh: Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 fighters
articles.content_orig:
A Houthi missile attack on the al-AIam military camp in southern Yemen has killed at least 50 people, according to local authorities.
The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles on Monday at the camp in Shabwa governorate during a training exercise, a spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces said.
Officials for the internationally-recognised government and medical sources initially said at least 18 people were killed and more than 30 wounded when the strike hit the facility, at which new security recruits were undergoing training.
However, the numbers have now risen dramatically. The local authority in Shabwa said later on Monday that 53 people had been killed and 200 injured, news agencies reported.
The attack was carried out as fighting continued to rage across Yemen. The civil war with between the Saudi-backed government and rebel Houthis was frozen for some years before the United States and Israel’s war on Iran provoked a return to conflict.
The hostilities escalated rapidly when the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded with a counteroffensive and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-aligned group seized in 2014.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Aramco.
On Monday, Saudi authorities sent alerts to residents of the capital Riyadh warning of “a hostile aerial threat”.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, said those killed in Shabwa were new recruits and promised a “firm response”.
“Targeting recruits reflects the Houthi militia’s approach of resorting to terrorist attacks when under pressure,” he said.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
“The Houthis said the attack targeted what they called a ‘Saudi-backed’ military base, referring to Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces who are stationed at military camps across the country,” he said.
“The Houthis say they will continue to target those bases. Spokesperson Yahya Saree says anywhere with a Saudi-backed military presence will be considered a legitimate target.”
Earlier, Yemeni government forces said they targeted Houthi gatherings, vehicles and weapons in al-Aqroudh, al-Shaqab and al-Sarari, south of Taiz, which is suffering from fuel shortages and soaring prices.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
articles.title_zh: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the frontlines by drone.
The “historic” mission comes just as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia .
Shared by the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade on Monday, the video shows the soldier strapping himself into a large drone and being flown at what appears to be relatively low altitude over blurred-out territory. The drone carefully lowers him down and the drone operator greets him with “Welcome back to the ground!” The video also showed blurred faces of drone operators who carried out the mission.
The post said the unidentified infantryman was wounded while at his position. “Due to intense enemy drone activity and the presence of landmines, evacuation using conventional unmanned ground vehicles was impossible,” the brigade said.
Injured Ukrainian soldier rescued with a drone
“At that point, the specialists in our unit took it upon themselves to attempt something that had never been done before: evacuating a serviceman using an aerial drone,” it added.
The craft used was a heavy-lift hexacopter, it said, originally designed as a bomber by a Ukrainian manufacturer. It looks about twice the size of the soldier in the video.
The specialists working on the mission had to ensure the drone could carry a human being without flipping over or swaying excessively, according to the unit.
The rescued soldier is currently undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, the brigade added. The squad leader and programmer with the brigade, only identified by his call sign Napalm, called the soldier a “hero” for agreeing to the mission, “having seen and heard the kind of machine that had arrived to get him.”
In a separate statement, Ukraine’s Ground Forces said its drone units are already conducting operations “that were recently considered science fiction.”
The war has increasingly become a technological arms race, with both Ukraine and Russia relying on drones to reduce human casualties.
The conflict has taken a severe toll on both armies, although neither side reports up-to-date numbers of those killed, injured or missing. Ukraine in particular has faced a severe shortage of manpower as it has tried to ramp up recruitment.
Ukraine had a major leap in drone technology this year, allowing it to limit Russian logistics in occupied territories as well as strike deeper inside Russia to target Russian oil refineries , commercial warehouses and data centers .
“This mission proves once again that Ukrainian service members, working in tandem with Ukrainian manufacturers, are setting global trends in the conduct of warfare,” the brigade’s statement added.
Despite hoping that its drone innovation would give it the upper hand at the negotiating table, Kyiv has faced pressure from the U.S. to halt its strikes on Russian oil sites after President Donald Trump signed a diesel deal with the Kremlin earlier this month.
Kyiv has since also reported gaps in intelligence sharing and restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is crucial for its drone missions, battlefield communications and air defense.
The drone evacuation comes just days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the Ukrainian government had approved an “experimental project” to use drones for medical logistics. Koretskyi said flights would require coordination with the military, and drones would be given a special status and would be identifiable in the air.
“During the war, moving medical cargo by road can cost critical time, especially for transplants,” he said. “Drones will be able to carry medicines, medical products, blood samples, and donor organs between hospitals, including from remote areas.”
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Some iPhone Duo orders getting moved up to earlier dates
articles.title_zh: Some iPhone Duo orders getting moved up to earlier dates
articles.content_orig:
iPhone Duo became available for pre-order last Friday, then quickly became backordered into late January 2027. However, a number of users have started reporting that their orders now show earlier delivery dates than originally estimated.
If you ordered an iPhone Duo last week, there’s a chance Apple has just moved up your delivery date—especially, it seems, if you‘re in Japan.
Over the weekend, a variety of iPhone Duo orders in Japan started getting pushed up to earlier dates than Apple originally estimated.
For example, here’s a user whose December date got moved up to October 23.
iPhone Duo、12月着のはずが発売日着に……!? 心とおサイフの準備ができてない！！！ pic.twitter.com/Aw1xepVQLA
Here’s a collection of similar reports found by 9to5Mac’s Dylan McDonald:
Apparently iPhone Duo shipping dates are being bumped up in Japan?? 👀👀 pic.twitter.com/mw8w07tVf8
It is unclear whether this change is going to start rolling out more broadly around the world. Though some orders arriving sooner than expected wouldn’t be surprising .
Apple has yet to comment on the updated shipping dates. It’s possible the improved delivery estimates end up being errors that get reverted, but hopefully that’s not the case.
So far the new dates appear limited to orders directly from Apple. We’ll keep you posted on any new developments to the story.
Has your iPhone Duo delivery date changed at all since ordering? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Donnie Wahlberg says he survived plane skidding incident
articles.title_zh: Donnie Wahlberg says he survived plane skidding incident
articles.content_orig:
LAS VEGAS ( FOX5 ) — A plane holding Donnie Wahlberg and multiple others skidded off a runway at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas on Sunday morning, prompting a ground stop and multiple delays at the airport.
The FAA issued a ground stop for the airport and two runways were closed after officials say a general aviation aircraft skidded off Runway 1L upon departure around 11 a.m. and made contact with a perimeter fence.
The ground stop has since been lifted and runways 1R and 1L have reopened after inspections were completed. Officials added that there were no injuries.
On Sunday night, actor Donnie Wahlberg posted a social media video clarifying that he was aboard the plane involved in the incident.
“Yes, it was me and my team/friends onboard the aircraft. It was a rather intense few moments (which felt like a few long minutes),” his caption read. “Thankful to God, of course, and to our incredible pilots who did an amazing job of keeping us safe and avoiding a serious disaster. The airplane did take some lumps — but we did not.”
Prior to the stop being lifted, departure traffic destined for Harry Reid was experiencing delays averaging an hour and 10 minutes, according to the FAA.
“Travelers are encouraged to check with their airlines regarding flight status,” airport officials said.

articles.title_orig: France’s Far Right Seizes the Moment as Rioting Stuns the Country
articles.title_zh: France’s Far Right Seizes the Moment as Rioting Stuns the Country
articles.content_orig:
The French prime minister has called for "very limited" and "localized" curfews after France's worst rioting in years
PARIS -- The French prime minister called for “very limited” and “localized” curfews Monday after a weekend marred by France’s worst rioting in years that targeted city halls , other public buildings and thousands of businesses across the country.
Speaking after an emergency meeting with senior government officials, Sébastien Lecornu defended police handling of the unrest, saying that “despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle.”
He said details of the curfews would be announced later Monday after consultations with mayors.
Mass protests in France are often tainted by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. Saturday’s unrest recalled the riots that followed the fatal police shooting of a teenager in 2023, when authorities imposed local curfews, and violence during the yellow vest movement that began in 2018 over fuel prices and broader economic grievances.
The prime minister's instructions come after Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation Sunday, but President Emmanuel Macron refused it “given the need for continued command of law enforcement in the current context,” Macron's office said in a statement Monday.
He instructed Nuñez “to take all necessary steps to ensure full transparency about the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that led to the violence,” the statement said.
Macron also asked for the introduction of “new policing tactics on the ground as quickly as possible” to put an end to the violence.
On Sunday evening, groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities. That followed the violence during nationwide protests Saturday against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools . At least 2,400 people were arrested across the country.
Authorities estimated Monday that at least 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted in several cities.
In Marseille, the prefect banned any protest or other gatherings from noon to 8 p.m. Monday.
“I submitted my resignation because I am responsible for everything that is happening,” Nuñez said on France Inter radio. “Now the real issue is ensuring that this doesn’t happen again. … We obviously need to be better at anticipating the kind of mobilization that is unfolding."
Nuñez blamed the violence on “hordes of troublemakers and looters” and “far-left activists,” and said police strategy needs to be adapted “in the face of extremely mobile groups.” Authorities said groups of hundreds of people sought confrontations with police and targeted public buildings, including city halls and other public offices.
Nuñez acknowledged that authorities had “lost control” in some major cities Saturday.
“You can’t look shopkeepers in the eye when hundreds of businesses have been looted and say we haven’t lost control in some of these major cities,” Nuñez said.
Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.
On Monday, cleanup crews and firefighters cleared shattered glass and other debris from the streets of Paris.
Ouri Zagoury, owner of a video game shop near Paris' Place de la République, said he closed the store Saturday afternoon but then saw looters forcing their way in on surveillance cameras.
“There were so many people coming in and out. And even though I called the police, they said not to intervene, that they would come, but they never did, which is another problem," Zagoury said.
Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally, pointed to the government's failure to prevent violence.
“The government has failed, the head of state has failed in his essential duty of protecting the French people,” he told reporters at party headquarters.
“I call on the people of France now, beyond their right to protest, to use their voting power,” Bardella said. He is campaigning alongside far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whose polling numbers have for months suggested she is the front-runner in next spring's presidential election.
Associated Press journalists Tom Nouvian, Oleg Cetinic and Nicolas Garriga in Paris and Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Priest killed by falling crucifix during live streamed Mass
articles.title_zh: Priest killed by falling crucifix during live streamed Mass
articles.content_orig:
A Catholic priest in Ecuador has died after he was fatally crushed by a falling crucifix while live-streaming evening mass.
The shocking accident occurred on Saturday at the Nuestra Senora del Perpetuo Socorro Church in Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city, some 265km southwest of the capital.
Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari was broadcasting the event live from his social media accounts when the mounted cross on the wall behind him fell suddenly, around 30 minutes into the stream.
Graphic footage of the mass showed a heavy crucifix hanging behind the altar detaching and falling onto the back of the priest's head.
Patricio Sánchez Molinari was killed by a cross while live streaming Catholic Mass (Facebook / Patricio Sánchez)
The priest was facing the congregation at the time and did not appear to see it fall. The video showed he did not stand up again after being struck.
The priest was knocked below the altar and out of view, but recorded horrified worshippers shouting out and rushing to his aid.
"Father, Father! Call an ambulance!" people could be heard shouting just before the broadcast cut out. Others could be seen rushing towards the altar to help the stricken cleric.
Emergency services were immediately called to the scene, but first responders were unable to revive the priest. The video of the livestream was later taken down from the priest's page, but circulated widely on social media, NBC News reported.
The archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed his death on Sunday, writing that Sanchez "has left to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory".
The priest was hosting evening mass when he was hit by the cross on the wall behind him (Facebook / Patricio Sanchez)
"Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon him. May he rest in peace. Amen," they wrote in a statement in Latin published on social media.
The archdiocese did not say what had caused the crucifix to fall or whether there would be an investigation.
It was unclear whether he was killed instantly or died later from injuries.
Sánchez belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic religious order founded in 1732 with a presence in 80 countries, according to the Associated Press.
A Eucharist in his memory was scheduled for Sunday evening, the archdiocese said.
Local authorities were yet to comment on the incident, and it was not clear what caused the crucifix to fall.
In 2014, a 21-year old man died and his friend was injured after they were crushed by a crucifix erected in honour of Pope John Paul II in northern Italy . The same year, a mother of two died in Chicago, US, after a stone gargoyle fell three stories from an old church, striking her as she was taking a walk with her fiancé.

articles.title_orig: Some smartphones will soon start acting more like a Google Pixel, but is that a good thing?
articles.title_zh: Some smartphones will soon start acting more like a Google Pixel, but is that a good thing?
articles.content_orig:
Pause Point , the mindfulness intervention Scrolling Break feature unveiled earlier this year as a Google Pixel 11 exclusive, is now expanding beyond Google’s own ecosystem, landing on third-party mobile devices.
Android’s new Pause Point functions more like an interactive speed bump. When the system detects an extended, passive scrolling session in endless feeds, it actively halts the app’s UI and presents an explicit interruption.
Instead of locking you out, it forces a decision: select a specific timeframe to continue or close the app and step away. What makes this rollout noteworthy isn’t just the feature’s design, but its sudden expansion.
Android Authority recently spotted Pause Point running natively on a OnePlus 13R running ColorOS 17 Beta. That single appearance tells us plenty about Google’s underlying delivery pipeline.
While support pages still list the Pixel 11 series as the exclusive home for the tool, functional integration into a deeply customized OEM skin confirms that Google is decoupling Pause Point from hardware-specific dependencies.
The move mirrors Google’s broader strategy with Android 17: centralizing core behavioral features inside the main Digital Wellbeing system container rather than tying them to Pixel Launcher binaries.
As Android 17 QPR updates reach wider distribution over the coming months, expect Pause Point to become a standard platform feature rather than a hardware selling point.
Samsung users should be ready to tackle doomscrolling with the new Android feature. It should be coming for Galaxy owners through an update to the Google Play system.
The company is also expanding One UI 9.0 software across Galaxy devices. You can check the new feature’s availability through Settings > Digital Wellbeing.
Google is polishing Android 17 QPR2 for a potential Galaxy S27 launch
Meet Yash, author and dynamic creator of the compelling tech narratives at Sammy Fans. He has evolved from a Samsung firmware aficionado to a multi-faceted tech storyteller. 

Yash's expertise shines brightest with his explorations into Samsung's One UI. Beyond the screen, his love for landscapes and rivers adds a unique flavor to his work.
Google bringing these 4 new scam protection features to Android phones
Samsung rolls out redesigned SmartThings app for Android
WhatsApp expands privacy with new Restricted chat feature
Android Auto 17.8 prepares for Google’s Magic Cue AI
YouTube users on Android report a bug that covers the progress bar
Here’s when One UI 9.0 official update coming to global markets
Galaxy S27 series will launch with One UI 9.5, and Samsung could use Android 17 QPR2 as a base for the software. Ahead of December release, Google is perfecting the operating system, which is crucial for Samsung’s next hardware.
Besides, Google is running Beta testing on Android 17 QPR3 version. It is crafted to shape the next Feature Drop for Pixel devices. This version would be available on eligible devices around March 2027 when Galaxy S27 series releases.
This year, Samsung’s Galaxy S26 series shipped with One UI 8.5. Findings revealed that that version is built on Android 16 QPR2, rather than the original OS. QPR2 was the minor release Google promised to bring to the ecosystem.
Based on that, Samsung might utilize Android 17 QPR2 for One UI 9.5. It would first land on Pixel devices by the end of the year as a major Feature Drop. Samsung, on the other hand, could ship it with Galaxy S27 series by March 2026.
Google last week released the Android 17 QPR 2 Beta 7 software. That update brought Pixel phones closer to the Stable release, thanks to the two major improvements linked to battery and download manager on Pixel devices.
On October 16, Google pushed Android 17 QPR 2 Beta 7.1 update for Pixel devices. The incremental release comes with a single improvement. However, the impact of that fix is not limited to just improving the user experience.
Frequent releases indicate that Google is seriously working on the minor Android 17 drop. It is expected to bring improvements to the overall experience, while enhancing core functions and reliability for eligible devices.
Google is rolling out a fix for Android Auto users who cannot see mobile network signal bars on their car screens. The missing icon made it difficult for drivers to check whether their phones had a strong or weak network connection.
Several users on Reddit recently reported that the signal icon had returned to their car displays. Users with different smartphones and cars are starting to see it again. However, the fix has not reached everyone yet.
The problem started after an Android Auto update removed the signal icon. Other features, such as Google Maps, phone calls, and music streaming, continued to work. However, when a song stopped playing or Maps stopped loading, drivers could not easily tell whether a weak network was the reason.
Google has acknowledged the problem and started rolling out a fix. If the signal bars are still missing, users should check the Google Play Store for updates to Android Auto and Google Play Services.
However, updating these apps may not fix the problem immediately. Google may also need to enable the fix through its servers, so some users will have to wait.
The rollout is expected to take time and could last several weeks. For now, keeping your apps updated is the best step. The return of the signal bars will help drivers check their mobile network connection more easily while using Android Auto.
Google is expanding its Android Earthquake Alerts System to more than 200 countries and regions to help people stay safe during earthquakes. Since its launch in 2021, the system has sent over one billion alerts to Android users worldwide.
The system uses Android phones to detect earthquake activity and send warnings to people in affected areas. These alerts can give people a few seconds to take cover before strong shaking begins.
Earlier, the service was available in 98 countries and regions. It is now expanding to more than 200 locations, including Panama, Guatemala and many others.
Android users in supported areas can receive three types of alerts: Be Aware, Be Ready and Take Action. Each alert provides information based on the expected strength of the earthquake.
Google is also improving the Be Ready alert with new features. In the coming months, users will see a map showing the area where shaking has been detected, the estimated earthquake magnitude, and steps they can take to stay safe.
These changes aim to help more people prepare for earthquakes. Although alerts cannot prevent earthquakes, even a few seconds of warning can help people take cover and protect themselves and their families.
Google is doubling down on its efforts to safeguard users, with the latest upgrade offering four new scam protection features to compatible Android phones and tablets.
Financial fraudsters have long abandoned obvious typo-ridden text messages and crude robocalls. Today’s cybercriminals rely on AI voice cloning and spoofed bank numbers that mimic reality down to the last digit.
Recent YouGov data commissioned by Google reveals that roughly 40% of users feel anxious about fraud. Independent testing by Leviathan Security Group shows that out-of-the-box threat handling remains uneven across Android and iOS.
To close these security gaps, Android is rolling out four distinct upgrades designed to intercept sophisticated social engineering before it inflicts damage.
Enhanced protection mode in Google Messages
The first pillar of this defense arrives inside Google Messages via a new opt-in setting called enhanced protection mode .
When activated, it routes complex conversation streams through Google’s cloud-based Gemini models using Private AI Compute, allowing the system to dissect a scammer’s intent without exposing private user data.

articles.title_orig: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won’t want to
articles.title_zh: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won’t want to
articles.content_orig:
Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift . For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced , and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro .
But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.
That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.
I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.
As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)
That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150 . The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines , I thought it sounded kind of fun.
That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.
The best starting place is Relativty VR . This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.
But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD , Project North Star , and the full-body tracking SlimeVR . There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.
A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.
The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders— Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.
Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.
Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.
The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.
Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.
You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.
My total spend for all that came to just under $180.
Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.
I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.
You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.
Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.
Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.
Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.
Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.
As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.
Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.
You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.
That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.
This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in the

articles.title_orig: Roche returns to China’s Hansoh for $15B biobucks ADC pact
articles.title_zh: Roche returns to China’s Hansoh for $15B biobucks ADC pact
articles.content_orig:
A year after their first antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) team-up, Roche has returned to Hansoh Pharmaceutical for a mammoth $15 billion biobucks pact.
The latest agreement spans a “broad portfolio of ADC programs,” Hansoh explained in an Oct. 19 release. They include two ADCs already in preclinical development at the Chinese biopharma, along with multiple programs focused on targets suggested by Roche but powered by Hansoh’s ADC tech.
The plan is for Jiangsu-based Hansoh to take these programs through phase 1 trials, before passing over responsibility to Roche to develop the ADCs worldwide—excluding Greater China.
In return, Hansoh will receive $400 million in upfront cash, followed by $110 million on the first anniversary of the deal. Further down the line, the biopharma is in line for potentially up to $15 billion in development, regulatory and commercialization milestones, as well as tiered royalties on sales if any ADCs make it to market.
The deal also has a clause where Hansoh could opt to contribute toward the global development of two programs from the collaboration. If it picks this route, Hansoh would become eligible to receive “incremental upside from the commercialization of these two programs,” according to the release.
This morning’s deal comes a year after Roche handed $80 million to Hansoh and pledged $1.45 billion in biobucks for the ex-China license to a CDH17-targeted ADC, dubbed HS-20110. At the time, HS-20110 was already in phase 1 testing in China and the U.S. as a potential treatment for colorectal cancer and other solid tumors.
“Building on the ADC partnership we announced last year, we are delighted to further strengthen our collaboration with Roche,” Eliza Sun, Executive Director of Hansoh’s board, said in this morning’s release.
“This new agreement reflects our shared commitment to advancing ADC innovation and underscores our strategy of leveraging our deep expertise to accelerate the development of transformative therapies for cancer patients globally,” Sun added.
Boris Zaïtra, head of corporate business development at Roche, said in this morning’s release that“expanding our strategic collaboration with Hansoh marks an important step in advancing our ADC vision.”
“Exploring next-generation ADCs is one of the most compelling frontiers in oncology today, offering the opportunity to address critical unmet needs and accelerate potential therapies for patients worldwide,” Zaïtra added.
Roche isn’t the only Big Pharma that’s turned to Hansoh to help power its ADC ambitions. GSK has already tasted clinical success with a pair of ADCs aimed at B7-H3 and B7-H4, respectively.
The B7-H3-directed ADC, dubbed ris-rez, recently achieved a median overall survival of 18.5 months in a phase 3 trial, lining up the therapy as a potential threat to Amgen and Merck & Co. in the lung cancer field. Last night, GSK unveiled the first global data for ris-rez, which demonstrated a 61% overall response rate in a phase 1b trial.
Jefferies analysts said that the readout helped move ris-rez from a therapy defined by its “impressive China phase 3” data to “a much more globally validated asset story.” Ris-rez is “starting to look like the B7-H3 ADC to beat in relapsed SCLC,” the analysts concluded.
Hong Kong-listed Hansoh has been one of the leading lights in China’s emergence as a biopharma innovation engine, notching collaborations with the likes of Merck & Co. and Regeneron . In August, Hansoh offered a bullish assessment of China’s innovative biopharma sector, arguing (PDF) that the industry is “fully transitioning from the ‘follower’ phase to the ‘frontrunner’ phase.”
This year, Hansoh stepped up spending to support its pipeline of more than 40 innovative medicine candidates that it is assessing in more than 70 clinical trials. R&D spending at the company jumped 20.7% to 1.7 billion Chinese yuan ($253 million) over the first half of the year.

articles.title_orig: US and China compete for influence in Central Asia
articles.title_zh: US and China compete for influence in Central Asia
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in Uzbekistan promoting trade and ties with Central Asia
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in Uzbekistan on Monday to promote trade and ties with Central Asia, during a trip that came amid rumblings that America’s top diplomat is ignoring pressing matters in favor of politically safer visits and meetings.
The trip, which involves a stop in India later this week, seeks to promote U.S. economic and security ties with Central and South Asia . But it has only tangential links to the Trump administration’s current main foreign policy dilemmas in the Middle East and with the Russia-Ukraine war .
Rubio has brushed aside suggestions he is eschewing the most difficult issues in favor of taking on lower-hanging diplomatic fruit with less risk of failure and political damage, and the State Department pushed back on the criticism of his schedule.
In Samarkand, Rubio was meeting with his counterparts from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan under the C5+1 diplomatic forum, which brings together the five Central Asian countries and the United States to discuss security, trade and other shared concerns.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the meeting, Rubio said “the United States wants to be a strong partner in Central Asia.”
“Central Asia has just not gotten the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now,” he said.
Despite repeated assurances from multiple administrations that the U.S. would become more actively involved in Central Asia, the region has often languished as a foreign policy priority in Washington.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the newly independent Central Asian nations saw a brief surge in U.S. interest, but that waned until after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States, which turned America’s attention once again toward Afghanistan and its neighbors.
The U.S. established a military presence in several countries mainly as transit points for equipment, materiel and provisions needed by U.S. and allied forces fighting the Taliban and al-Qaida in Afghanistan.
As the U.S. wound down its 20-year operation in Afghanistan, the Trump administration, in both its first and second terms, has sought to elevate its ties with Central Asia due to its location between Russia and China, but also as an underdeveloped area ripe for U.S. business opportunities.
Rubio’s trip, which has been heavily promoted by the U.S. ambassador to India and special presidential envoy for Central Asia, Sergio Gor, is perhaps the most ambitious U.S. attempt in decades to boost economic and commercial ties with the region. Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Rubio described “an incredible delegation” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining.
“Historically, Central Asia has been the crossroads for trade between the West and the East. And today, as part of a broader renaissance and global engagement, it stands once again to play that vital role in transnational commerce," he told officials at the meeting.
The region is "a new location for investment, and it serves as a new location for export, a central terminal out of which materials that are vital for the future of all nations are being delivered,” he added.
President Donald Trump hosted their leaders at a White House summit last November, and announced more than $130 billion in commercial deals, including agreements for regional airlines to purchase Boeing aircraft.
The administration has also been keen to get the Muslim majority countries to join the Abraham Accords, which expanded the number of Arab states with diplomatic ties with Israel. Kazakhstan, which had already recognized Israel, is the only one of the five to sign the accords .
Associated Press writer Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.title_zh: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.content_orig:
A California woman who prosecutors allege was spying on a son of Taiwan’s president was indicted this month on charges of conspiracy and being an unregistered foreign agent for China.
The indictment was filed Oct. 9 in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the allegations it lays out mirror an earlier criminal complaint against the woman, Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine.
Prosecutors say Zhang, who also goes by Heather, spied on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his home in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. The spying is alleged to have taken place between roughly June and September 2025, prosecutors claim.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that is the source of 90% of the world’s “leading-edge chip manufacturing,” according to the U.S. International Trade Administration . China claims Taiwan, which the U.S. has no official relationship with , though it is required by law to ensure Taiwan can defend itself.
Prosecutors allege Zhang was under the direction of an unnamed Chinese government official and former classmate at her alma mater, China’s University of International Relations, which is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus,” an FBI investigator said in earlier court documents.
An example of the alleged activity was a request by the former classmate to send him pictures “of the house” where the son lives, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors alleged that Zhang flew from California to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area to conduct surveillance of the unidentified son and his home from outside.
The indictment alleges she captured photos, video and license plate information and sent them to the person alleged to be her Chinese handler. An unidentified person, who had fled to China in September, was with her, prosecutors said.
Zhang also traveled to China in August 2025 to meet with a Chinese government official, returned days later and told the official she would most likely be going to where the victim was the following week, according to the indictment.
Her lawyer, Craig Harbaugh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
Previously, Harbaugh, a veteran criminal defense attorney, described Zhang as an upstanding resident of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of Los Angeles, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said in court Oct. 7.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Sunday.
Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry, said this month after Zhang was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport that he was “not familiar” with the situation and that Beijing “opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative.”
U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim ordered Zhang held in pretrial detention after prosecutors argued she poses a flight risk. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons website shows that she remains in custody.
Zhang is scheduled to appear in federal district court Friday for a post-indictment arraignment. She could face up to 15 years in prison.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.title_zh: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
French officials are exploring introducing curfews as the country reels from its worst rioting in years after protests over education and the cost of living spiraled into a wave of deadly, country-wide violence that has sparked a blame game at home and threatens to spill over into its European neighbors.
Over the weekend, police fired tear gas into crowds and fought running battles with black-clad, hooded rioters who set fires and broke into shops and government buildings, with images showing historic buildings ablaze.
The mood in the country remained tense on Monday, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asking some cities to impose “partial curfews” to protect people, property and businesses. In Marseille, officials banned all gatherings and demonstrations from midday until 8 p.m. local time in anticipation of any more flare-ups, while protestors blocked access to the Louvre Museum in Paris, forcing it to close.
Those measures were introduced after more than 2,000 people were arrested this past weekend, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands. As France begins to count the cost, accusations are mounting that the government failed to adequately anticipate the scale of the crisis, with an election to succeed French President Emmanuel Macron just six months away.
The vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, authorities and political leaders stress – but the level of fighting and destruction , the worst seen in years, has shaken the nation and prompted forceful condemnations from leaders and the public alike.
“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said on Sunday evening. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”
He also promised to hold meetings this week to discuss “concrete proposals” and to listen to protesters’ demands. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to stem the protests in France – as well as similar demonstrations against costs of living now spreading in other countries nearby.
It started in September with a strike by students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs, who demanded more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.
Students around the country, long frustrated with an understaffed and overcrowded education system, launched protests that at times turned violent. A heavy-handed police response fueled public anger and pushed hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets, especially after videos of a police officer using a banned headlock on a girl.
Within a few weeks, the protests swelled to become a broader movement beyond students, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.
“This can’t go on,” said 57-year-old Maria Pallas, a member of a major French trade union, speaking to CNN at Saturday’s protest in Paris. “There’s the cost of living. There’s unemployment. There’s a bunch of things. A young person will go looking for work, we’ll promise him a lot, and he’ll end up with nothing.”
Over half a million people demonstrated across France on Saturday. For the most part, things were peaceful; far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the crowd in Paris as “moving calmly.”
But in several locations the protests spilled into violence, especially as night fell. In Paris, groups of masked young people looted shops and started fires; in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office; in the central city of Limoges, the spire of a 143-year-old town hall collapsed in flames, reviving painful memories for some of the Notre Dame Cathedral fire. Hundreds of businesses were vandalized across the Île-de-France region, which includes Paris, a local business representative told BFMTV.
The protests subsided somewhat on Sunday, with small pockets flaring, and police firing tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, one of the largest public squares in Paris.
By the end of the weekend, Paris looked like a “war zone,” one visitor to the city told Reuters. Residents across the capital were stunned, with some condemning the looters and rioters, and others placing blame with authorities who failed to address the crisis earlier.
“It’s heartbreaking, heartbreaking seeing our city like this,” said 59-year-old Marseille resident Farida, who did not give a last name, according to Reuters. “If every protest ends with all the shop windows smashed and stores trashed, this simply cannot go on — it cannot go on.”
One Paris resident, 56-year-old Paola Formenti, voiced support for the protesters’ “legitimate” anger, even as she condemned the violence.
In his Sunday address, Macron acknowledged protesters’ grievances and said he would take “a number of international initiatives” to tackle fuel prices and ensure a stable supply from Gulf nations. He did not make any concrete assurances or give further specifics.
Even interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted authorities had failed to anticipate the scale of the riots and offered his resignation, though Macron refused to accept it.
The protests and fallout could shape France’s upcoming election next spring. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed this weekend that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Mélenchon, has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.
Protesters have taken to the streets elsewhere in Europe this weekend, too.
In Belgium, students demonstrated against the state of their education system. In Lisbon, Portugal, tens of thousands of people marched on Saturday to protest rising costs of living and the country’s housing crisis.
In Italy, Milan also saw two consecutive nights of unrest this weekend. Protesters threw stones and looted supermarkets, while police responded with tear gas, and water cannons, and arrested 32 people.
Meanwhile in Albania, students have been taking to the streets for months, protesting perceived government corruption. Demonstrations in the capital Tirana turned violent this weekend, with one person photographed throwing a Molotov cocktail at riot police.
Authorities in many of these countries have condemned the violence and called for calm. The protests have caught the attention of the White House, with Vice President JD Vance posting a video of the burning Limoges town hall on X and blaming the unrest on failed immigration policy.
US President Donald Trump also mentioned the protests during a rally in Georgia this weekend, joking: “Let’s go to France and join the revolution and spend our $5,000 there,” referring to the dividend promised if the Republicans win the midterm elections.
CNN’s Joseph Ataman, Niamh Kennedy, Lisa Courbebaisse, Lucie Lepellec, Catherine Nicholls, Sana Noor Haq, James Legge, Sharon Braithwaite, and Melissa Bell contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China Lectures Israel on the West Bank: What About Tibet?
articles.title_zh: China Lectures Israel on the West Bank: What About Tibet?
articles.content_orig:
Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in Israel
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left the Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.
Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, was set upon last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupied West Bank towns.
The photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground,” Levine said. “Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me.” She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
Huckabee, a rightwing ally of President Donald Trump with a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine. In a post on X on Saturday, he noted that she was a US citizen who had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”
Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu , has been ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.
In an interview with the Associated Press on Sunday, Levine said she had been “shocked and insulted” to hear that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as “alleged”, adding that the prime minister “had all the evidence on the table”.
But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, and in a letter signed by several of the country’s top former security and intelligence officials, in which they all expressed shame over the attack.
Levine blamed “Jewish terrorists” for Thursday’s attack and added: “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today.”
The photojournalist also said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries. “I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this,” she said. “They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
The attack on the Palestinian farmers and Levine was followed on Saturday by another outbreak of settler violence directed against European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of the French city of Cambrai, who were visiting the occupied West Bank .
Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground. A masked militant shouted “Vive la France!” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Baudoux told Agence France-Presse after he was attacked. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening. For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.”
Violence is surging ahead of bitterly fought elections to be held on 27 October, with Palestinians’ annual olive harvest being repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement rightwing base.
France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has called on Israel to “urgently halt criminal violence” and to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux. The EU has condemned the attack and urged “full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists”.
The European Commission executive vice-president, Teresa Ribera, went further, posting an interview with Levine in hospital and adding the caption: “They want no witnesses.”
Israel’s foreign ministry has condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
On Monday, Israeli ⁠police said they have ⁠arrested ⁠eight ​suspects as part of an investigation ⁠into violent incidents in the West ⁠Bank over the weekend. The police did not identify the suspects.
Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, called Levine in hospital on Saturday, saying the attack was “outrageous and shocking” and was weighing on his conscience.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the elections, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, criticised the prime minister over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses”. He described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in a post on his Truth Social network on Sunday, hailing him as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He added: “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
The Washington Post has reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation into the attack on Levine, even though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.
Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says about 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report
